\section[i]{\ta{இ} — the letter that opens \ta{இல்லை}}

\label{lesson:TA-S127-letter-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: read \ta{உ} and \ta{ஓ} aloud, and write each once.

Now say \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} (\emph{illai}), \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one character out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{இ}}
\textbf{\ta{இ}} — \emph{i}.

It is the letter at the front of \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} (\emph{illai}), \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}, one of the first words in this book. You have been writing its \textbf{sign}, \ta{◌ி}, since \ta{நன்றி}. This is the \textbf{independent} shape of the same vowel: the one a word uses when it \emph{begins} with the sound.

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{இ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/TA-S127-letter-i-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ta{இ} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: curl around the inner loop
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, sweep down the inner right curve
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, carry left and turn through the lower loop
  \item \textbf{4.} without lifting, climb the lower diagonal
  \item \textbf{5.} without lifting, carry right and turn around the lower loop, then lift
  \item \textbf{6.} put the pen down again and climb the outer left side
  \item \textbf{7.} without lifting, arch over the top and down the right — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order, not a national standard — Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 4, \ta{இ} (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 192.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} and point at \ta{இ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{இ} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ta{ஓ}, then \ta{இ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{இ}? (\textbf{i}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ta{இல்லை}}, \emph{illai}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai]{\ta{◌ை} — the sign that ends \ta{இல்லை}}

\label{lesson:TA-S128-vowel-sign-ai}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: read \ta{ஓ} and \ta{இ} aloud, and write each once.

Now say \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} (\emph{illai}), \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one character out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{◌ை}}
\textbf{\ta{◌ை}} — \emph{ai}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}, not a letter. It attaches to a consonant and replaces the built-in \emph{a} with \emph{ai}. Look at the end of \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}}: the sign sits on the \textbf{left} of \ta{ல}, although you say it after. Tamil writes this sign first and sounds it second.

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{◌ை}}
Put your pen on \ta{◌ை} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} and point at \ta{◌ை} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{◌ை} three times, saying \emph{ai} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ta{இ}, then \ta{◌ை}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{◌ை}? (\textbf{ai}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ta{இல்லை}}, \emph{illai}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sa]{\ta{ஸ} — the letter inside \ta{நமஸ்காரம்}}

\label{lesson:TA-S129-letter-sa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: read \ta{இ} and \ta{◌ை} aloud, and write each once.

Now say \textbf{\ta{நமஸ்காரம்}} (\emph{namaskāram}), \textquotedblleft{}the borrowed bow-word\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one character out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ஸ}}
\textbf{\ta{ஸ}} — \emph{sa}.

It is inside \textbf{\ta{நமஸ்காரம்}} (\emph{namaskāram}), the borrowed bow-word you met beside \ta{வணக்கம்}. \ta{ஸ} is a \textbf{Grantha} letter: Tamil added it to write words that came from Sanskrit, so you will see it mostly in borrowed words.

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{ஸ}}
Put your pen on \ta{ஸ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ta{நமஸ்காரம்}} and point at \ta{ஸ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{ஸ} three times, saying \emph{sa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ta{◌ை}, then \ta{ஸ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{நமஸ்காரம்}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{ஸ}? (\textbf{sa}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ta{நமஸ்காரம்}}, \emph{namaskāram}, \textquotedblleft{}the borrowed bow-word\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
